_comment: Byte-exact encode/decode pairs for the kilnlink_frame envelope, shared across all three implementations (kilnlink C, App/drivers/espInterfaces/uart_protocol.c, pc_tools/src/kilnctrl/protocol.py). A test loading this manifest should: decode wire_hex and assert every decoded field matches, then re-encode from the fields and assert byte equality with wire_hex. Every value below was generated by pc_tools/src/kilnctrl/protocol.py (Frame.to_raw/stuff) 2026-08-16 and the first vector is independently cross-checked against kilnlink's own C implementation in test/test_frame.c -- see CommonFW/README.md 'Test vectors are the mechanism that keeps three implementations honest'.

vectors.name: data_with_payload
vectors.note: Cross-checked against kilnlink's own C implementation in test/test_frame.c (test_cross_implementation_vector) 2026-08-16 -- both agree byte-for-byte.

vectors.name: ack_zero_length_payload
vectors.note: Zero-length payload -- the frame is exactly header+CRC, no payload bytes at all.

vectors.name: payload_needs_escaping
vectors.note: Payload deliberately contains both bytes that must be byte-stuffed (0x7E, the frame delimiter, and 0x7D, the escape byte itself) plus an ordinary byte -- exercises the stuffing path, not just the header. wire_hex has 7 stuffed bytes where raw_hex has 5, from the two escaped bytes each becoming a 2-byte escape sequence.
vectors.wire_hex_note: raw_hex's 5-byte payload (017e027d03) becomes 7 bytes on the wire: 0x7e -> 7d 5e, 0x7d -> 7d 5d, the plain bytes 01/02/03 pass through unchanged

hostile_vectors.name: too_short
hostile_vectors.note: Fewer than HEADER_LEN(8)+CRC_LEN(2) bytes -- cannot even hold a header.

hostile_vectors.name: length_exceeds_max_payload
hostile_vectors.note: LENGTH byte (offset 7) is 254, past KILNLINK_FRAME_MAX_PAYLOAD (253). Must be rejected on this basis alone, before the buffer's actual size is even considered -- an attacker-controlled length byte must never drive an out-of-bounds read. Trailing bytes are padding, not a real CRC -- irrelevant since this is rejected before the CRC check runs.

hostile_vectors.name: length_mismatch
hostile_vectors.note: LENGTH byte says 5 payload bytes follow (needs 8+5+2=15 bytes total); the buffer is only 10 bytes, room for header+CRC and nothing else.

hostile_vectors.name: bad_crc
hostile_vectors.note: A structurally valid zero-length BROADCAST frame (type=4, msg_index=42, src=SAFETY/7, dst=ESP/7) with its low CRC byte flipped (0x60 -> 0x9F).

hostile_vectors.name: unknown_type
hostile_vectors.note: Type byte 0x99 is not DATA/ACK/NACK/BROADCAST. The trailing two bytes are a genuinely correct CRC over this exact header, so this tests the type check specifically, not a CRC false-positive.

hostile_vectors.name: unterminated_escape
hostile_vectors.note: A trailing 0x7D (ESC) with nothing following it -- an escape promises one more byte that never arrives. Checked on the stuffed/wire form via kilnlink_unstuff, not the raw decoder (there is no delimiter here at all, deliberately -- a decoder must not require one to detect this). kilnlink_unstuff treats this as an explicit error; pc_tools' protocol.py unstuff() does NOT -- it is documented as a one-shot test/decode convenience (the live RX path is FrameDecoder instead), and it silently drops a trailing dangling escape rather than raising. That is a real, known, low-stakes difference between the two implementations, not a bug in this vector -- kilnlink is the stricter one here because the isolated safety link has no equivalent of FrameDecoder's incremental resync to fall back on.
